cards.description: White argues Price’s analogy principle excludes divine action before evidence is heard, so rival historical methods should instead be compared for consistent evidential treatment.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White directly contests Price’s governing historical method by arguing that a principle of analogy can exclude divine action before evidence is assessed, and his appeal to consistency makes that methodological dispute clear and responsive. Principal limitation: Price expressly permits miracles while withholding automatic credibility from miracle reports, so White does not establish that this disciplinary restraint is covert metaphysical naturalism or that Price has barred every positive conclusion in advance. Live burden: White must supply publicly assessable criteria that can admit divine explanations when warranted while distinguishing them from competing supernatural claims under equally demanding historical standards. Locked score: The fixed 76 reflects a coherent, central, and notably responsive challenge whose force is reduced by modest evidential support and by its insufficiently charitable treatment of Price’s stated distinction.

cards.description: Price separates miracle possibility from Gospel accuracy, arguing that providential preservation assumes the historical reliability it is supposed to establish through independent evidence.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price uses Ladd’s providential-preservation claim to draw a responsive distinction between confessional assurance that the Gospels remained accurate and publicly assessable historical evidence for that accuracy. Principal limitation: The need for divine supervision does not itself show that distortion was ordinarily probable, and one cited preservation claim does not establish that evangelical apologetics generally depends on this controlling assumption. Live burden: Price must provide independent evidence of actual distortion and demonstrate that White’s reliability case rests on providence rather than manuscript evidence, contextual comparison, or other historical considerations. Locked score: The fixed 75 recognizes the move’s clear formulation, concrete target, and strong relevance to public warrant, while its weaker causal inference and broader characterization keep its logical coherence and evidential support below its responsiveness and precision.

cards.description: White distinguishes admitting supernatural claims from believing them, proposing consistent historical comparison and citing his critical treatment of Joseph Smith’s First Vision.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White’s Mormon comparison shows that admitting supernatural claims for historical examination does not require accepting them, while his call to use the exact same basis answers the charge that openness collapses into credulity. Principal limitation: Consistency remains too thin because agreement with a tradition’s message may establish internal fit without independently supporting an extraordinary event or showing why rival explanations are less probable. Live burden: He must specify cross-tradition standards for source independence, corroboration, probability, and alternatives, then demonstrate that New Testament and Mormon claims receive equivalent scrutiny. Locked score: The fixed 81 reflects strong coherence, responsiveness, relevance, and clarity, moderated by thinner evidential warrant and calibration because the comparison illustrates impartial admissibility more effectively than it supplies a complete method for deciding among miracle claims.

cards.description: Price likens history to meteorology: divine intervention may remain possible, yet unpredictable transcendent causes cannot receive ordinary evidential probabilities or historical tracing.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price’s meteorology analogy separates methodological restraint from metaphysical denial, allowing divine intervention while explaining why historians weigh traceable human causes, and answers White’s accusation that analogy assumes a closed naturalistic worldview. Principal limitation: The comparison concerns prediction, whereas historical inquiry works retrospectively, and unrepeatable causes can leave distinctive traces that permit evaluation even when their occurrence could not have been forecast. Live burden: Price must explain why alleged miracles cannot be assessed abductively from surviving evidence and identify what kind of trace could distinguish divine action from mythmaking or human explanations. Locked score: The fixed 82 rewards exceptional responsiveness, central relevance, a clear methodological distinction, coherence, and measured openness, while its more modest evidential warrant reflects the unsupported step from unpredictability to historical untraceability.

cards.description: White closes by treating both approaches as worldview-laden and asks listeners to compare their consistency rather than imagine Price’s criticism is entirely presupposition-free.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White candidly acknowledges his own commitment to scriptural authority while identifying Price’s contrary methodological commitment, turning the exchange toward a direct comparison of how each worldview handles historical evidence. Principal limitation: Internal consistency cannot alone define truth, because an elaborate but false system may remain coherent while failing facts outside itself, so White’s proposed test does not establish scriptural authority. Live burden: White must connect biblical coherence to independently constrained historical evidence and show that apparent counterexamples are resolved without selective harmonization, while judging rival explanations by the same demanding standards. Locked score: The fixed 76 reflects a clear, relevant, and responsive methodological challenge, tempered by weaker evidential warrant and calibration because consistency usefully tests a worldview yet cannot independently verify its conclusions.

cards.description: Price makes historical confidence decline with temporal distance and evidential scarcity, contrasting ancient uncertainty with massively corroborated modern events such as Dachau.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price gives a calibrated account of historical knowledge as probabilistic and revisable, using the contrast between massive modern corroboration and sparse ancient evidence to answer the charge that his method entails total skepticism. Principal limitation: Temporal distance is only a rough proxy for evidential weakness, and Price does not individually assess the strongest New Testament sources by their quantity, independence, genre, or preservation, leaving his general caution underapplied. Live burden: Price must show how his probability standard evaluates those particular sources and competing explanations without allowing theological commitment or methodological preference to predetermine the result. Locked score: The fixed 84 reflects strong coherence, responsiveness, clarity, and especially calibration, while stopping short of a higher rating because the evidential case remains general where the debate requires source-specific historical analysis.

cards.description: White rejects Price’s Hadith analogy because major collections arose centuries after Muhammad, unlike the comparatively early documentary foundation he attributes to New Testament writings.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White isolates a temporal disanalogy in Price’s comparison, arguing that hadith collections arose roughly 250 to 270 years after Muhammad while New Testament documents, on White’s dating, stand nearer their events and retain earlier material. Principal limitation: That contrast depends on the disputed chronology White asserts and does not establish that shorter transmission prevented pious attribution, especially without comparing oral layers, community controls, attribution incentives, and intermediary evidence across the traditions. Live burden: White must defend his Gospel dates and show, through historical evidence, that proximity produced effective correction rather than merely reducing the time available for development. Locked score: The fixed 80 reflects a coherent and responsive challenge to an important analogy, tempered by moderate evidential warrant, incomplete comparison, and overstatement in declaring no parallel.

cards.description: Price argues that imagining vigilant disciples suppressing invented reports is not evidence they successfully policed tradition, and reasoning backward from desired reliability is circular.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price distinguishes a conceivable eyewitness safeguard from evidence that living disciples consistently detected and suppressed invented reports, exposing the inferential gap where mere possibility was used to guarantee uncontaminated tradition. Principal limitation: His critique remains negative and offers little affirmative evidence about how reports circulated, when witnesses intervened, which communities could coordinate correction, or whether partial eyewitness constraint operated without comprehensive policing. Live burden: Price must map circulation routes, named witnesses, competing communities, and documented correction episodes to estimate the safeguard’s reach while allowing that limited controls could constrain some developments. Locked score: The fixed 81 recognizes high responsiveness, clarity, coherence, and charitable calibration in denying a guarantee rather than asserting certain distortion, while reduced evidential support prevents the forceful conceptual objection from ranking higher.

cards.description: White argues that “kicking against the goads” was conventional Greek expression, so shared wording cannot establish that Acts borrowed its conversion narrative from literature.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White weakens Price’s borrowing inference by identifying four earlier uses of ‘kicking against the goads’ and using the ‘pulling my leg’ analogy to show why an idiom can recur without literary dependence. Principal limitation: This rebuttal addresses shared wording but never compares the fuller Heliodorus and Pentheus episodes with Acts, so Price’s proposed parallels in narrative structure, sequence, or motif remain untested. Live burden: White must examine the strongest alleged correspondences and show that common idiom, widespread motif, genre convention, or independent narration explains them at least as well as direct borrowing. Locked score: The 85 reflects unusually clear, coherent, and responsive reasoning against one concrete datum, supported by earlier usage evidence, while withholding higher credit because the broader source comparison needed to decide Price’s claim is absent.

cards.description: Price names a modest contemporaneous eyewitness letter as evidence that would change his mind, while treating the Gospel residue as too myth-shaped for confidence.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price answers the charge that his position excludes contrary evidence by naming an attestation that would persuade him, while conceding its absence may be accidental and Jesus may be irretrievable rather than nonexistent. Principal limitation: Requiring a surviving papyrus letter sets a demanding threshold for an ancient figure, and Price does not show that Pauline, Gospel, non-Christian, and reception evidence is inadequate under historical comparisons. Live burden: Price must defend why this benchmark is appropriate and explain, source by source, how myth-shaped narration prevents the existing record from supporting a historical core without treating documentary silence as decisive. Locked score: The 80 rewards strong responsiveness, clarity, and cautious calibration, but remains below the top tier because the criterion’s comparative warrant and application to the wider evidence are underdeveloped.

cards.description: Price invokes Parry and Lord to argue oral recitation is fresh performance with flexible wording and order, not verbatim preservation of an original.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price turns the modern-orality evidence against verbatim preservation by connecting variable phrasing and reordered material to Parry and Lord’s observation that each recitation is a new performance, answering the proposed transmission model. Principal limitation: Balkan epic performance shows that oral skill can coexist with recomposition, but does not demonstrate that short Jesus teachings, catechesis, or controversy traditions developed similarly, nor identify which meanings would remain stable across performances. Live burden: Map the comparison onto gospel traditions and specify testable expectations for stable themes, altered wording, and reordered sequence while weighing rival transmission models under equal historical standards. Locked score: The 82 reflects strong coherence, evidence use, responsiveness, and relevance, tempered by an analogy whose reach beyond the studied performance setting remains unproved.

cards.description: White announces that Price’s authorship and transmission theory is undemonstrated and conflicts with consistent interpretation, but initially supplies only a roadmap for later support.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White identifies a standard by insisting that Price’s authorship and transmission reconstruction must cohere with authorial purpose and the extant manuscript record before displacing a historical reading. Principal limitation: This passage announces that Price’s theory is incapable of demonstration or defense and contradicted by the data, yet supplies no literary seam, manuscript finding, dated comparison, or account of Price’s internal evidence to establish those categorical judgments. Live burden: Present passage-level conflicts and transmission evidence that distinguish White’s reconstruction from Price’s, then show why those materials favor one explanation without assuming the disputed chronology. Locked score: The 63 recognizes a centrally relevant roadmap and a demand for explanatory fit, but its evidential warrant, precision, responsiveness, and calibration remain limited because the promised supporting argument has not appeared.

cards.description: Price argues diaspora Judaism’s cosmopolitan setting made scriptural and Greek literary materials jointly available, so mixed source use by Gospel authors remains culturally coherent.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price answers White’s incompatibility objection with synagogue art, funerary imagery, a treatment of Ezekiel, awareness of foreign gods, and Maccabean conflict, showing that Jewish communities could encounter scriptural and Hellenistic materials without sealed cultural worlds. Principal limitation: These examples establish availability and interaction, not evangelists’ dependence on Homer, Euripides, or pagan gods, while differing regions and periods weaken their representativeness for the authors and audiences at issue. Live burden: Price must date each comparator, establish plausible authorial access, identify distinctive textual correspondences, and show that borrowing explains them better than shared Jewish traditions or cultural knowledge. Locked score: The fixed 80 reflects a coherent, concrete, highly responsive rebuttal that keeps mixed-source composition plausible, but compressed chronology and the unproven path from contact to dependence prevent a stronger rating.

cards.description: White argues early Jewish monotheism makes a pagan dying-god template implausible, while Price’s strongest archaeological examples substantially postdate Jesus and Jerusalem’s destruction.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White confronts Price’s availability argument by distinguishing awareness of pagan cults from willingness to construct a Messiah through dying-and-rising-god patterns, while adding that the synagogue evidence postdates the earliest Christian setting. Principal limitation: The reasoning treats early Jewish monotheism too uniformly, because resistance does not eliminate selective adaptation, polemical transformation, or diversity among pre-seventy communities, and the dating objection does not dispose of every Hellenistic influence invoked. Live burden: White must document relevant early communities, connect their commitments to particular New Testament authors and audiences, and explain early Christology through Jewish developments while comparing alternatives by equal historical standards. Locked score: The fixed 79 rewards clear relevance, strong responsiveness, and chronological counterevidence, while its broad cultural generalization and incomplete exclusion of adapted influence constrain its warrant and calibration.

cards.description: Price cites tensions about divine knowledge and women speaking as internal evidence that Pauline letters contain editorial layers rather than one continuous authorial context.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price grounds his compositional case in concrete tensions, contrasting knowing only Christ crucified with knowing God's depths and comparing permissions and prohibitions concerning women speaking, thereby supplying literary evidence after the manuscript challenge. Principal limitation: He compresses the passages, neglects their rhetorical and local contexts, and treats one thematic contrast as virtually impossible for one author although contextual variation remains a substantial alternative, so his examples suggest interpolation without establishing it. Live burden: Price must show that contextual reconciliation fails for each passage and that layered composition predicts their particular wording and placement better than unitary authorship. Locked score: The 74 reflects a responsive, text-specific hypothesis with meaningful evidential contact, reduced by abbreviated exegesis, overstatement, and failure to discriminate decisively between interpolation and contextual explanation.

tags.label: Confirmation bias
tags.context: it would sure explain an awful lot if the text had been interpolated

cards.description: White uses Price’s differently styled books to show audience, genre, and context can explain variation without requiring separate authors or later textual interpolation.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White challenges the inference from difference to multiple authors through Price's differently styled books, whose explanation by genre and audience demonstrates that one writer can vary across contexts. Principal limitation: The analogy establishes possibility rather than Corinthian history, and White neither reconstructs the missing circumstances nor explains each cited tension about knowledge and women speaking, while Price's consistency objection remains unanswered. Live burden: White must derive plausible contexts from the letter, apply them consistently to every alleged discontinuity, and show that contextual variation explains the wording and placement better than interpolation. Locked score: The 82 rewards coherent, clear, and responsive exposure of an underdetermined authorship inference, while withholding higher credit because the analogy does not provide the case-specific historical and textual explanation needed to resolve the disputed passages.

cards.description: Price treats Paul’s silence about the Damascus road and alleged Heliodorus and Pentheus parallels as evidence that Acts constructed the detailed conversion scene.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price joins Paul’s silence about Acts’ Damascus-road narrative to named Heliodorus and Pentheus stories, giving his literary-origin proposal concrete comparators and evidential focus rather than bare suspicion. Principal limitation: Letters need not recount biography, and asserting similarity does not supply distinctive, ordered correspondences that separate borrowing from ordinary idiom, shared motifs, genre convention, or independent narration, while the spoken First Corinthians reference remains unresolved. Live burden: Price must compare the narratives directly, establish Luke’s access, identify unlikely conventional parallels, and explain why Paul’s brief revelation language conflicts with rather than merely omits the later account. Locked score: The fixed 68 rewards a relevant, responsive, source-specific challenge with recognizable evidence, while its undeveloped comparison, gap from resemblance to dependence, and limited testing of plausible alternatives constrain its force.

cards.description: White asks why late authors would forge letters under Paul’s name if no authentic writing or recognized ministry had previously given that name authority.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White identifies pressure within wholesale late pseudonymity: writers seeking authority by using Paul’s name seemingly presuppose that it already carried enough recognition among Christian communities to make attribution useful. Principal limitation: Such standing does not establish authorship of the canonical letters, because a historical or legendary Paul could gain authority through oral memory, missionary reputation, factional tradition, or later stories, so the challenge narrows Price’s theory without refuting it. Live burden: White must show why that reputation requires earlier epistolary activity and why nonliterary or legendary routes cannot adequately explain the forgers’ choice. Locked score: The fixed 84 reflects a logically sharp, responsive challenge exposing a causal obligation for Price, tempered by modest direct evidence and the unresolved distinction between Paul’s antecedent standing and authorship of surviving letters.

cards.description: Price speculates that a polemically developed Paul related to Simon Magus and later Gnostic reception could supply authority before the canonical letters appeared.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price answers why late writers would invoke Paul by proposing that a preexisting Paul–Simon figure, reinforced through polemical and Gnostic reception, supplied authority, while candidly calling the proposal speculative rather than established history. Principal limitation: The proposed identity remains thinly supported because the chronology, patristic testimony, Justin’s silence, and relationships among Pauline, Simonian, Marcionite, and Gnostic traditions are compressed and contested, so the parallels do not demonstrate that this persona existed before the letters. Live burden: Establish a dated chain of independent evidence connecting these figures and communities, then show that this reconstruction explains Pauline authority better than conventional historical-Paul accounts under comparable standards. Locked score: The 69 reflects a responsive, carefully qualified possibility whose calibration cannot overcome its unresolved chronology, uncertain identity link, and limited historical warrant.

cards.description: White argues independently branching manuscript streams would preserve First Corinthians versions without verses 3–11 if that passage entered only through later interpolation.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White makes the manuscript tradition a historical test, arguing that branching transmission and tenacious variant readings should preserve traces of a major interpolation, while surviving witnesses contain no manuscript stream without First Corinthians 15:3–11. Principal limitation: The inference assumes branching preceded the alteration, because an insertion made before recoverable streams diverged could pass unanimously into later witnesses and leave exactly the uniform record White cites, despite not belonging to the earliest text. Live burden: Date the relevant branch points and compare expected survival of passage-free witnesses under early-insertion, late-insertion, and original-text models, applying equivalent preservation assumptions throughout. Locked score: The 86 recognizes a clear, highly responsive argument grounded in observed manuscript behavior, but stops higher because absent variants constrain later interpolation without independently excluding alteration before recoverable branching.

cards.description: Price notes Paul was misrepresented during his lifetime and disputed writings gained ancient followers, undermining confidence that contemporaries reliably suppressed distorted Christian traditions.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price grounds his challenge to apostolic policing in examples, pairing Paul's complaints about distortion during his lifetime with divided reception of disputed writings to show that correction and proximity did not ensure uniform transmission. Principal limitation: These counterexamples establish misrepresentation and contested attribution, but not that central claims were durably replaced or lost, or that the cited communities fed the canonical transmission streams at issue. Live burden: He must trace durable corruption into those streams and show why that explanation fits the surviving historical pattern better than preservation amid ordinary disagreement. Locked score: A 75 reflects a coherent, responsive, source-focused challenge with useful historical analogies, tempered by weaker evidential linkage and calibration because the examples support transmission risk more clearly than the claimed scale or persistence of corruption.

cards.description: White argues unusually varied early papyri contradict a centralized Christian standardization capable of erasing every First Corinthians witness lacking the disputed resurrection passage.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White answers Price's standardization escape route by linking variation among early papyri to the pattern expected from uncontrolled copying, while explaining why coordinated erasure should produce more uniform descendants. Principal limitation: Diversity among surviving witnesses after putative standardization cannot exclude earlier editorial convergence before extant genealogical branches formed, especially if a localized common archetype supplied later streams. Live burden: He must connect measured variation to independence predating the alleged insertion and distinguish that history from descent through a shared edited ancestor, while sustaining the claim that a version lacking First Corinthians 15:3–11 should leave alternative lines. Locked score: An 86 reflects responsiveness, coherence, and substantial evidential force, reduced by the unresolved timing and ancestry inference.

cards.description: Price argues First Corinthians 15:3–11 interrupts the resurrection treatise and combines rival apostolic credential lists, offering internal evidence of a later editorial compromise.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price answers the manuscript challenge with concrete internal evidence, identifying changed function, apostolic credentials, the grouping of Peter, James, the Twelve, and all apostles, and apparent redundancy as signs of editorial compromise. Principal limitation: These features do not uniquely indicate insertion, because Paul’s announced gospel gives verses 3 through 11 a plausible role in the resurrection argument, while an expanded list can unite witnesses without preserving competing factions. Live burden: Price must show that removing the passage improves the chapter and that editorial compromise explains the grouped credentials better than continuous composition despite no surviving manuscript without these verses. Locked score: The score of 80 reflects a specific, responsive, clearly articulated internal case with genuine evidential force, bounded by a strong contextual alternative and no external textual corroboration.

cards.description: White presses Price to explain how every early manuscript branch without First Corinthians 15:3–11 vanished despite an interconnected and visibly diverse transmission tradition.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White converts the dispute into a transmission-history test by asking why a text without verses 3 through 11 survives in none of the interconnected manuscript streams, directly confronting a consequence of Price’s reconstruction. Principal limitation: This absence is powerful negative evidence but not conclusive, because an insertion before every recoverable branch separated could leave surviving streams with the passage even if an earlier form existed. Live burden: White must establish that relevant branching predates the proposed insertion, or show why some pre-insertion lineage should have survived, without treating unanimous witnesses as certainty. Locked score: The score of 88 recognizes an exceptionally direct, coherent, well-supported challenge that sharply raises Price’s burden, while stopping short of a higher rating because the chronology needed to exclude universal early adoption remains unproved.

cards.description: White argues Galileans understood Roman crucifixion as a death march, so Jesus could demand taking up one’s cross before his own later execution.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White gives the cross metaphor a concrete pre-crucifixion setting by explaining that Galileans could recognize Roman crucifixion as terror and understand the call as self-denial joined to a death march. Principal limitation: Showing that the words were intelligible before Jesus died establishes a possible reading, but not that Jesus uttered them, while their fit with later Christian reflection leaves retrospective formulation or reshaping a live alternative. Live burden: The argument must compare wording and narrative placement across traditions and show that pre-event origin explains them better than later composition under demanding historical standards. Locked score: The score of 83 reflects a clear, responsive contextual rebuttal with strong coherence and precision, moderated by limited direct warrant for utterance and the unresolved possibility that later resonance influenced the received form.

cards.description: Price compares John, Mark, Matthew, Luke, and Acts to show the temple-destruction saying receives divergent attribution, narrative setting, and interpretation across traditions.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price anchors his developmental account in a concrete comparison among John's bodily interpretation of the temple saying, its false-witness placement in Mark and Matthew, and Luke's related treatment through Stephen. Principal limitation: These differences make interpretive development plausible but do not demonstrate incompatible judgments about one identical sentence, because distinct speakers, purposes, and narrative settings could produce complementary selections without textual distortion. Live burden: The argument must establish sufficiently identical variants and show that expectation-driven transmission explains their divergent handling better than contextual attribution or complementary narrative choice, with alternatives tested by the same historical standards. Locked score: The score of 79 rewards specific cross-canonical evidence, direct relevance, and an auditable comparative inference, while remaining constrained because logical compatibility persists and alternative narrative explanations receive too little consideration.

cards.description: White reads Matthew 10’s Jewish restriction as an early ministry stage and Matthew 28’s worldwide commission as post-resurrection expansion, rather than contradiction.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White supplies a coherent narrative sequence, distinguishing the restricted mission during Jesus’s Jewish ministry from the post-resurrection worldwide commission, while noting that Acts summarizes rather than reproduces discussion, so its silence cannot sustain Price’s conclusion. Principal limitation: This reading establishes compatibility rather than authenticity, and because Acts never clearly invokes the decisive commission during the controversy, White does not fully explain why remembered instructions from Jesus left little visible trace in the reasoning. Live burden: He must show that Matthew inherited both stages instead of harmonizing rival traditions and compare this explanation directly with Price’s community-composition account under equally demanding historical standards. Locked score: The 87 reflects a clear, responsive rebuttal with strong coherence, tempered by limited evidence for inheritance and the unresolved burden concerning Acts.

cards.description: Price links Matthew’s opposed mission instructions to Jewish-only and Gentile-supporting communities, while conceding that a plausible fabrication mechanism does not prove actual fabrication.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price anchors his hypothesis in identifiable texts, connects Matthew’s opposed mission instructions to the Jewish–Gentile controversy, and concedes that an attribution mechanism does not prove either saying was invented. Principal limitation: His inference from Acts’ silence is too strong because the narrative selectively reports discussion, successive mission stages remain plausible, and comparison with fabricated Islamic traditions is suggestive but insufficiently developed to establish the same process in Matthew. Live burden: He must justify why Acts favors community composition over selective reporting, answer White’s chronological distinction, and provide firmer evidence linking each directive to its proposed constituency. Locked score: The 75 recognizes concrete textual support, relevance, and qualification, while reflecting the underdetermined leap from later controversy and narrative silence to rival invented sayings and the incompletely defended comparative analogy.

sections.title: Inspiration, meaning, and the Bible's value

cards.description: White argues biblical claims differ fundamentally from Apollonius traditions in worldview and coherence, so admitting divine speech need not collapse every miracle account together.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White rejects the choice between excluding divine action in advance and accepting every miracle story alike, arguing that Apollonius and Scripture differ in worldview and narrative consistency while reconnecting the dispute to whether God has spoken. Principal limitation: He asserts those fundamental differences and biblical consistency without presenting paired examples, defining a coherence test, or showing why coherence establishes historical truth or divine authorship rather than literary unity. Live burden: Compare specific claims from Philostratus and Scripture under equal historical standards, identify measurable differences, and explain why the better supported account warrants the theological conclusion. Locked score: The 76 reflects a coherent, responsive comparative reply with clear relevance to the motion, tempered by thin displayed evidence, undefined criteria, and an inferential gap between consistency and divine speech.

cards.description: Price argues ethical and literary value survives disputed authorship or textual secondary status, citing admired passages that he regards as meaningful later additions.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price separates a passage’s origin, authorship, canonical status, inspiration, and present value, using secondary examples to show that critical conclusions need not erase literary, moral, or theological worth. Principal limitation: That distinction preserves value but does not establish biblical unreliability, identify whether any disputed saying is original, or defeat White’s historical claim, leaving its contact with the motion supportive rather than decisive. Live burden: Connect the independence of value from provenance to a reason for rejecting the motion while recognizing why provenance matters when a text is offered as historical testimony. Locked score: The 83 rewards clear distinctions, concrete examples, charitable calibration, and responsiveness to the claim that criticism leaves no treasures, while withholding stronger credit because the argument clarifies Price’s position more than it proves unreliability.

cards.description: White presents sustained coherence across roughly fifteen centuries and forty authors as experiential support for Scripture’s unity, while explicitly labeling the appeal as personal testimony.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: White identifies the claim as testimony and connects sustained engagement with skeptical scholarship to perceived harmony across many authors and centuries, making the appeal relevant and appropriately modest about its experiential basis. Principal limitation: He provides few concrete cross-author examples or independent tests showing that the coherence is better explained by divine unity than by canon selection, inherited tradition, or interpretive harmonization, leaving the central inference underdetermined. Live burden: He must exhibit specific convergences that survive historical and literary scrutiny, accommodate genuine textual diversity, and outperform rival explanations under equally demanding standards. Locked score: The score of 75 reflects a clear, charitable, responsive affirmation whose cumulative reasoning bears directly on biblical unity, while its testimonial form and limited public evidence prevent it from establishing the stronger divine conclusion.

tags.label: Subjective validation
tags.context: there is a beauty to the harmony of God's word that absolutely amazes me

cards.description: Price argues mandatory infallibility blocks plausible readings of error, tension, and uneven quality, whereas critical interpretation can still preserve the Bible’s genuine profundities.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Price separates appreciation of biblical profundity from assent to inspiration and argues that mandatory infallibility constrains interpretation in advance, offering a coherent rationale for preserving possibilities such as error, contradiction, and uneven literary quality. Principal limitation: His phone-book comparison chiefly exposes crude dictation models, while differences in literary merit neither entail factual error nor demonstrate that sophisticated contextual accounts of inspiration force inferior readings. Live burden: He must identify passages where inerrancy excludes the best explanation and compare those cases fairly with nuanced views allowing genre, human authorship, and textual diversity. Locked score: The score of 83 reflects a forceful, charitable, directly relevant closing synthesis with clarity and responsiveness, tempered by an analogy that reaches beyond what it proves and insufficient case-specific evidence for the broader interpretive indictment.

ai: Biblical credibility is best defended cumulatively through manuscript resilience, contextual coherence, and disciplined comparison rather than by using inspiration as an evidential shortcut.
Early textual diversity makes coordinated standardization erasing every contrary First Corinthians form substantially less probable than stable inheritance through independent branches.
Apparent contradictions should first be tested against narrative sequence, audience, genre, and rhetorical setting before becoming evidence of composite authorship.
Supernatural claims can enter historical comparison without automatic credit when identical evidential standards govern Christian and rival religious traditions.
Common motifs and conventional phrases establish cultural availability but cannot demonstrate borrowing without distinctive ordered correspondences and plausible authorial access.
A cumulative case strengthens when independent textual, contextual, and comparative considerations converge without requiring one argument alone to establish inspiration.
Therefore the affirmative modestly supports biblical historical reliability, although divine authorship still requires criteria connecting preservation and coherence to genuine divine speech.
Branching before doctrinal convenience

Independent manuscript branches make interpolation costly when their separation predates the controversy that would motivate adding the resurrection list. If geographically separated witnesses already contain First Corinthians 15:3–11 before any coordinating authority could align them, the hypothesis must posit either repeated independent adoption or an insertion in an exceptionally early shared archetype. Those alternatives should then be tested against the persistence of other variants across the same branches. Agreement does not prove that no lost form ever existed, because surviving witnesses cannot reveal every stage of transmission. It does, however, shift the burden: interpolation must explain both the passage’s early distribution and the absence of a recoverable contrary stream.
Context must predict

Contextual harmonization earns evidential weight when it risks predictions instead of merely dissolving an apparent tension after the fact. Reading the mission commands as successive stages predicts an Israel-focused restriction during Jesus’s ministry, a worldwide commission after the resurrection, and later disagreement about how that expansion should be implemented rather than whether Gentiles could ever be included. Matthew, Luke, and Acts can then be examined for that ordered pattern. If the sequence consistently explains both changed scope and subsequent dispute, context supplies a reason to prefer development within one narrative over community invention. If the texts resist those predictions, however, the same test strengthens Price’s compositional explanation rather than insulating harmony from failure.
One miracle comparison grid

Extraordinary reports should be compared through one shared set of questions: how close the sources are to the events, whether witnesses are independent, whether opponents corroborate anything, how stable the narrative remains, what background knowledge bears on it, and whether ordinary alternatives explain it. Applying that grid to the resurrection, Mormon visions, Hadith reports, and Apollonius keeps supernatural causation eligible without granting it automatic credit. If the New Testament performs better, that advantage follows from the comparison rather than from treating its own theological message as a criterion of truth. The grid therefore disciplines judgment while leaving its outcome genuinely evidential and provisional.
Biblical reliability remains underdetermined when theological guarantees, flexible oral transmission, literary development, and harmonization can each conceal uncertainty within the surviving record.
Permitting miracles does not make particular reports historically probable when divine causation supplies no independently traceable signature for disciplined assessment.
Eyewitness proximity is merely a possible safeguard unless evidence shows witnesses encountered, recognized, and successfully corrected developing reports across communities.
Oral traditions can preserve themes while recomposing wording and sequence, so continuity of message cannot simply equal verbatim historical recollection.
Internal tensions and culturally available literary models remain compositional alternatives even when no surviving manuscript preserves a proposed earlier form.
Inerrancy can distort comparative judgment whenever it excludes error or unevenness before individual passages receive evidence-sensitive evaluation.
Therefore confidence should remain passage-specific and provisional, preserving biblical value while declining comprehensive historical or divine reliability for the collection.
Eyewitness control needs a denominator

Eyewitness proximity supplies a possible corrective mechanism, but isolated cases of correction cannot show how reliably it governed a wider tradition. That inference requires a denominator: how many reports reached identifiable witnesses, how often those witnesses challenged them, which challenges were preserved, and what circulated beyond their authority. Paul’s limited control over representations of his teaching and the divided reception of disputed writings make systematic policing less safe to assume, without proving that distortion prevailed everywhere. Mapping circulation, rival receptions, and correction episodes would therefore convert reassurance into bounded confidence. Until then, the evidence warrants neither perfect eyewitness control nor unrestricted invention.
Transmission tests can disagree

Manuscript agreement and literary fit bear on different stages of a passage’s history. Agreement among surviving witnesses makes a late interpolation less likely, because the passage had already entered their recoverable common ancestry. Yet that agreement cannot by itself show that the common ancestor contained no earlier editorial addition. Conversely, a contextual seam can support an early-redaction hypothesis, but it does not neutralize unanimous external attestation or establish when the proposed change occurred. The rational conclusion is comparative and provisional: confidence in interpolation should rise only when a dated compositional account explains the alleged seam while also bearing the historical cost imposed by stable transmission.
Two ledgers for value and origin

Historical origin and present value come apart because they depend on different evidence and standards. If a saying was added later, it may lose force as testimony about what Jesus said while retaining philosophical, literary, or spiritual merit in what it teaches. If it is authentic, that pedigree alone does not make its teaching wise or humane. Keeping two ledgers prevents either judgment from covertly deciding the other: textual criticism can revise claims about provenance without declaring a passage worthless, and admiration cannot convert canonical acceptance into historical proof. The distinction therefore preserves critical openness while explaining how doubt about authorship can coexist with serious appreciation of the Bible.

        The Bible is true
        James White
      

      
        Strengthened final argument
        Biblical credibility is best defended cumulatively through manuscript resilience, contextual coherence, and disciplined comparison rather than by using inspiration as an evidential shortcut.
        
          
                
                  Premise 1
                  Early textual diversity makes coordinated standardization erasing every contrary First Corinthians form substantially less probable than stable inheritance through independent branches.
                
              
                
                  Premise 2
                  Apparent contradictions should first be tested against narrative sequence, audience, genre, and rhetorical setting before becoming evidence of composite authorship.
                
              
                
                  Premise 3
                  Supernatural claims can enter historical comparison without automatic credit when identical evidential standards govern Christian and rival religious traditions.
                
              
                
                  Premise 4
                  Common motifs and conventional phrases establish cultural availability but cannot demonstrate borrowing without distinctive ordered correspondences and plausible authorial access.
                
              
                
                  Premise 5
                  A cumulative case strengthens when independent textual, contextual, and comparative considerations converge without requiring one argument alone to establish inspiration.
                
              
        
        
          Conclusion
          Therefore the affirmative modestly supports biblical historical reliability, although divine authorship still requires criteria connecting preservation and coherence to genuine divine speech.
        
      

      
        New reinforcing arguments
        
          
                
                  Branching before doctrinal convenience
                  Independent manuscript branches make interpolation costly when their separation predates the controversy that would motivate adding the resurrection list. If geographically separated witnesses already contain First Corinthians 15:3–11 before any coordinating authority could align them, the hypothesis must posit either repeated independent adoption or an insertion in an exceptionally early shared archetype. Those alternatives should then be tested against the persistence of other variants across the same branches. Agreement does not prove that no lost form ever existed, because surviving witnesses cannot reveal every stage of transmission. It does, however, shift the burden: interpolation must explain both the passage’s early distribution and the absence of a recoverable contrary stream.
                
              
                
                  Context must predict
                  Contextual harmonization earns evidential weight when it risks predictions instead of merely dissolving an apparent tension after the fact. Reading the mission commands as successive stages predicts an Israel-focused restriction during Jesus’s ministry, a worldwide commission after the resurrection, and later disagreement about how that expansion should be implemented rather than whether Gentiles could ever be included. Matthew, Luke, and Acts can then be examined for that ordered pattern. If the sequence consistently explains both changed scope and subsequent dispute, context supplies a reason to prefer development within one narrative over community invention. If the texts resist those predictions, however, the same test strengthens Price’s compositional explanation rather than insulating harmony from failure.
                
              
                
                  One miracle comparison grid
                  Extraordinary reports should be compared through one shared set of questions: how close the sources are to the events, whether witnesses are independent, whether opponents corroborate anything, how stable the narrative remains, what background knowledge bears on it, and whether ordinary alternatives explain it. Applying that grid to the resurrection, Mormon visions, Hadith reports, and Apollonius keeps supernatural causation eligible without granting it automatic credit. If the New Testament performs better, that advantage follows from the comparison rather than from treating its own theological message as a criterion of truth. The grid therefore disciplines judgment while leaving its outcome genuinely evidential and provisional.
                
              
        
      
    
  
            
    
      
        Biblical reliability is unestablished
        Robert Price
      

      
        Strengthened final argument
        Biblical reliability remains underdetermined when theological guarantees, flexible oral transmission, literary development, and harmonization can each conceal uncertainty within the surviving record.
        
          
                
                  Premise 1
                  Permitting miracles does not make particular reports historically probable when divine causation supplies no independently traceable signature for disciplined assessment.
                
              
                
                  Premise 2
                  Eyewitness proximity is merely a possible safeguard unless evidence shows witnesses encountered, recognized, and successfully corrected developing reports across communities.
                
              
                
                  Premise 3
                  Oral traditions can preserve themes while recomposing wording and sequence, so continuity of message cannot simply equal verbatim historical recollection.
                
              
                
                  Premise 4
                  Internal tensions and culturally available literary models remain compositional alternatives even when no surviving manuscript preserves a proposed earlier form.
                
              
                
                  Premise 5
                  Inerrancy can distort comparative judgment whenever it excludes error or unevenness before individual passages receive evidence-sensitive evaluation.
                
              
        
        
          Conclusion
          Therefore confidence should remain passage-specific and provisional, preserving biblical value while declining comprehensive historical or divine reliability for the collection.
        
      

      
        New reinforcing arguments
        
          
                
                  Eyewitness control needs a denominator
                  Eyewitness proximity supplies a possible corrective mechanism, but isolated cases of correction cannot show how reliably it governed a wider tradition. That inference requires a denominator: how many reports reached identifiable witnesses, how often those witnesses challenged them, which challenges were preserved, and what circulated beyond their authority. Paul’s limited control over representations of his teaching and the divided reception of disputed writings make systematic policing less safe to assume, without proving that distortion prevailed everywhere. Mapping circulation, rival receptions, and correction episodes would therefore convert reassurance into bounded confidence. Until then, the evidence warrants neither perfect eyewitness control nor unrestricted invention.
                
              
                
                  Transmission tests can disagree
                  Manuscript agreement and literary fit bear on different stages of a passage’s history. Agreement among surviving witnesses makes a late interpolation less likely, because the passage had already entered their recoverable common ancestry. Yet that agreement cannot by itself show that the common ancestor contained no earlier editorial addition. Conversely, a contextual seam can support an early-redaction hypothesis, but it does not neutralize unanimous external attestation or establish when the proposed change occurred. The rational conclusion is comparative and provisional: confidence in interpolation should rise only when a dated compositional account explains the alleged seam while also bearing the historical cost imposed by stable transmission.
                
              
                
                  Two ledgers for value and origin
                  Historical origin and present value come apart because they depend on different evidence and standards. If a saying was added later, it may lose force as testimony about what Jesus said while retaining philosophical, literary, or spiritual merit in what it teaches. If it is authentic, that pedigree alone does not make its teaching wise or humane. Keeping two ledgers prevents either judgment from covertly deciding the other: textual criticism can revise claims about provenance without declaring a passage worthless, and admiration cannot convert canonical acceptance into historical proof. The distinction therefore preserves critical openness while explaining how doubt about authorship can coexist with serious appreciation of the Bible.
